questions.question: State the approximate percentage of nitrogen in present-day dry air.
questions.modelAnswer: About 78%.
markingPoints: About 78%.

questions.question: State the approximate percentage of other gases in present-day dry air.
questions.modelAnswer: About 1%, mainly argon with a very small amount of carbon dioxide.
markingPoints: About 1%, mainly argon with a very small amount of carbon dioxide.

questions.question: State the approximate percentage of oxygen in present-day dry air.
questions.modelAnswer: About 21%.
markingPoints: About 21%.

questions.question: State the approximate composition of dry air and calculate the oxygen volume in 2.40 dm3 of air.
Explain how ice-core and sediment evidence can be used to reconstruct past atmospheric composition and climate.
questions.modelAnswer:
Trapped air bubbles preserve samples of past atmosphere.
Isotope ratios and sediment/pollen records act as climate proxies.
Layers can be dated.
Agreement between independent records increases confidence, but resolution and dating uncertainty limit conclusions.
markingPoints: Trapped air bubbles preserve samples of past atmosphere.
Isotope ratios and sediment/pollen records act as climate proxies.
Layers can be dated.
Agreement between independent records increases confidence, but resolution and dating uncertainty limit conclusions.

questions.question: Name the main gas believed to have formed Earth’s early atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Why was there little or no oxygen in Earth’s early atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: There were no photosynthesising organisms initially, and any oxygen produced reacted with rocks/minerals.
markingPoints: There were no photosynthesising organisms initially, and any oxygen produced reacted with rocks/minerals.

questions.question: Explain why scientists use cautious language about the early atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: It formed billions of years ago, so direct evidence is limited and models may change.
markingPoints: It formed billions of years ago, so direct evidence is limited and models may change.

questions.question: Describe the likely composition of the early atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with small amounts of methane and ammonia, and little or no oxygen.
markingPoints: Mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with small amounts of methane and ammonia, and little or no oxygen.

questions.question: Explain how the early atmosphere changed as oceans and sedimentary carbonate rocks formed.
questions.modelAnswer:
Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to oceans.
CO₂ dissolved in oceans and was used by marine organisms.
Carbon became locked in shells/skeletons and carbonate sediments/rocks, reducing atmospheric CO₂.
markingPoints: Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to oceans.
CO₂ dissolved in oceans and was used by marine organisms.
Carbon became locked in shells/skeletons and carbonate sediments/rocks, reducing atmospheric CO₂.

questions.question: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in the presence of light and chlorophyll).
markingPoints: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in the presence of light and chlorophyll).

questions.question: How did photosynthetic algae and plants change Earth’s atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: They absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis, decreasing CO2 and increasing O2 over time.
markingPoints: They absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis, decreasing CO2 and increasing O2 over time.

questions.question: Explain how photosynthetic organisms altered atmospheric gases and enabled complex animal life.
questions.modelAnswer:
Photosynthesis removed CO₂ and released O₂.
Oxygen accumulated, enabling efficient aerobic respiration.
It also enabled ozone formation, reducing harmful UV at Earth’s surface.
markingPoints: Photosynthesis removed CO₂ and released O₂.
Oxygen accumulated, enabling efficient aerobic respiration.
It also enabled ozone formation, reducing harmful UV at Earth’s surface.

questions.question: Explain how atmospheric oxygen increased and why it did not immediately accumulate when photosynthesis began.
questions.modelAnswer:
Algae/plants photosynthesised, releasing O2.
Initially reacted with iron/rocks and other reducing materials/respiration.
Accumulated only after sinks became saturated/production exceeded removal.
markingPoints: Algae/plants photosynthesised, releasing O2.
Initially reacted with iron/rocks and other reducing materials/respiration.
Accumulated only after sinks became saturated/production exceeded removal.

questions.question: How did oceans help reduce the concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and became locked into carbonate sediments and rocks.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and became locked into carbonate sediments and rocks.

questions.question: Explain three processes that decreased atmospheric carbon dioxide over geological time.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dissolved in oceans.
Photosynthesis removed CO2.
Carbonate shells/sediments formed limestone.
Carbon buried in fossil fuels/rocks.
Explain storage/removal.
markingPoints: Dissolved in oceans.
Photosynthesis removed CO2.
Carbonate shells/sediments formed limestone.
Carbon buried in fossil fuels/rocks.
Explain storage/removal.

questions.question: Name three greenhouse gases.
questions.modelAnswer:
Carbon dioxide
Methane
Water vapour.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide
Methane
Water vapour.

questions.question: Explain how greenhouse gases warm Earth’s surface.
questions.modelAnswer:
Short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth.
The surface emits infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface.
markingPoints: Short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth.
The surface emits infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface.

questions.question: Distinguish between a greenhouse gas and an atmospheric pollutant.
questions.modelAnswer: A greenhouse gas absorbs outgoing infrared radiation and contributes to warming. An atmospheric pollutant is a substance in air that harms health or the environment.
markingPoints: A greenhouse gas absorbs outgoing infrared radiation and contributes to warming. An atmospheric pollutant is a substance in air that harms health or the environment.

questions.question: Explain why a substance can be both a greenhouse gas and an atmospheric pollutant.
questions.modelAnswer: A substance can have more than one effect. For example, carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and high concentrations can affect the environment; nitrogen oxides can contribute to warming and harm health.
markingPoints: A substance can have more than one effect. For example, carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and high concentrations can affect the environment; nitrogen oxides can contribute to warming and harm health.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect as an energy-transfer sequence without saying greenhouse gases trap sunlight.
questions.modelAnswer:
Short-wave solar radiation passes/absorbed by surface.
Earth warms.
Emits long-wave IR.
Greenhouse gases absorb IR and re-emit in all directions.
Less net energy escapes, increasing surface temperature.
markingPoints: Short-wave solar radiation passes/absorbed by surface.
Earth warms.
Emits long-wave IR.
Greenhouse gases absorb IR and re-emit in all directions.
Less net energy escapes, increasing surface temperature.

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation
markingPoints: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase atmospheric methane.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: cattle/rice farming, landfill and leaks during fossil-fuel extraction.
markingPoints: Examples: cattle/rice farming, landfill and leaks during fossil-fuel extraction.

questions.question:
A policy reduces methane emissions quickly but CO2 only slowly.
Explain why methane reduction can affect near-term warming while long-lived CO2 still matters.
questions.modelAnswer:
Methane strong greenhouse gas but shorter atmospheric lifetime.
Cuts can reduce near-term forcing.
CO2 accumulates/persists, so long-term warming depends on cumulative emissions.
markingPoints: Methane strong greenhouse gas but shorter atmospheric lifetime.
Cuts can reduce near-term forcing.
CO2 accumulates/persists, so long-term warming depends on cumulative emissions.

questions.question: Link human activities to increases in carbon dioxide and methane, giving at least two sources of each.
questions.modelAnswer:
CO2: fossil-fuel combustion, deforestation, cement.
CH4: cattle, rice, landfill, fossil-fuel extraction.
Explain release/reduced uptake where relevant.
markingPoints: CO2: fossil-fuel combustion, deforestation, cement.
CH4: cattle, rice, landfill, fossil-fuel extraction.
Explain release/reduced uptake where relevant.

questions.question: Evaluate the statement: “A correlation between atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature proves CO₂ is the only cause.”
questions.modelAnswer:
Correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors affect climate.
However, greenhouse mechanism is established and multiple independent records/models support a CO₂ contribution.
Data uncertainties and confounding variables should be considered.
“only cause” is unjustified.
markingPoints: Correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors affect climate.
However, greenhouse mechanism is established and multiple independent records/models support a CO₂ contribution.
Data uncertainties and confounding variables should be considered.
“only cause” is unjustified.

questions.question: State two possible effects of global climate change.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two: rising sea levels; changing rainfall patterns; more extreme weather; loss of habitats; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity.
markingPoints: Any two: rising sea levels; changing rainfall patterns; more extreme weather; loss of habitats; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity.

questions.question: Why is peer review important when scientists publish climate research?
questions.modelAnswer: Other experts check the methods, evidence and reasoning, helping identify errors and improve confidence in conclusions.
markingPoints: Other experts check the methods, evidence and reasoning, helping identify errors and improve confidence in conclusions.

questions.question: State three possible consequences of global climate change.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: sea-level rise, changing rainfall, more extreme weather, habitat loss, migration changes and reduced biodiversity/food security.
markingPoints: Examples: sea-level rise, changing rainfall, more extreme weather, habitat loss, migration changes and reduced biodiversity/food security.

questions.question: A graph shows temperature rising while solar output has no matching long-term rise. Explain how this evidence should be used in an argument.
questions.modelAnswer:
Weakens solar-output explanation for trend.
Does not alone prove sole cause.
Combine with greenhouse mechanism, gas records and other forcings.
Distinguish correlation/evidence strength.
markingPoints: Weakens solar-output explanation for trend.
Does not alone prove sole cause.
Combine with greenhouse mechanism, gas records and other forcings.
Distinguish correlation/evidence strength.

questions.question: Evaluate the claim that a short period of cooler weather disproves global warming.
questions.modelAnswer:
Weather is short-term and local.
Climate is a long-term global pattern.
Natural variability can cause cool periods within a warming trend.
Use long-term global datasets rather than one event.
markingPoints: Weather is short-term and local.
Climate is a long-term global pattern.
Natural variability can cause cool periods within a warming trend.
Use long-term global datasets rather than one event.

questions.question: Explain why climate predictions have uncertainty but are still useful.
questions.modelAnswer:
Future emissions unknown.
Complex feedback/cloud/ocean behaviour.
Model resolution/data limits.
Natural variation.
Models tested against observations and give ranges/scenarios useful for risk decisions.
markingPoints: Future emissions unknown.
Complex feedback/cloud/ocean behaviour.
Model resolution/data limits.
Natural variation.
Models tested against observations and give ranges/scenarios useful for risk decisions.

questions.question: Evaluate the claim that correlation between CO2 and global temperature proves CO2 causes warming.
questions.modelAnswer:
Correlation alone not proof.
Confounders/feedback possible.
But known IR mechanism, lab evidence, historical data, models and multiple independent observations support causation.
Balanced evidence-based conclusion.
markingPoints: Correlation alone not proof.
Confounders/feedback possible.
But known IR mechanism, lab evidence, historical data, models and multiple independent observations support causation.
Balanced evidence-based conclusion.

questions.question: Explain why climate models should be tested against historical data before being used for projections.
questions.modelAnswer:
Historical data provide outcomes not used or partly used in development.
If a model reproduces observed patterns within uncertainty, confidence increases.
Failures reveal assumptions or processes needing revision.
markingPoints: Historical data provide outcomes not used or partly used in development.
If a model reproduces observed patterns within uncertainty, confidence increases.
Failures reveal assumptions or processes needing revision.

questions.question: Explain why correlation between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperature is not, by itself, complete proof of causation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Correlation can be influenced by other variables and feedbacks.
Causal confidence comes from mechanism, controlled/physical evidence, modelling and multiple independent datasets, not correlation alone.
markingPoints: Correlation can be influenced by other variables and feedbacks.
Causal confidence comes from mechanism, controlled/physical evidence, modelling and multiple independent datasets, not correlation alone.

questions.question: What is a carbon footprint?
questions.modelAnswer: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
markingPoints: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.

questions.question: Define carbon footprint and evaluate three ways a school could reduce it, including one limitation for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Total direct+indirect greenhouse gases as CO2e.
Measures such as insulation/efficiency, renewable electricity, transport change, lower consumption/food waste.
Evaluate cost, intermittency, behaviour, embodied impacts, feasibility and data.
markingPoints: Total direct+indirect greenhouse gases as CO2e.
Measures such as insulation/efficiency, renewable electricity, transport change, lower consumption/food waste.
Evaluate cost, intermittency, behaviour, embodied impacts, feasibility and data.

questions.question: How are nitrogen oxides formed in a vehicle engine?
questions.modelAnswer: At high temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react.
markingPoints: At high temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react.

questions.question: How is sulfur dioxide formed when fossil fuels burn?
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen during combustion.
markingPoints: Sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen during combustion.

questions.question: Explain why carbon monoxide is produced in a faulty gas heater and why it is dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer:
Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, forming CO.
CO is colourless/odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing blood oxygen transport and potentially causing death.
markingPoints: Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, forming CO.
CO is colourless/odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing blood oxygen transport and potentially causing death.

questions.question: State how carbon monoxide is formed during coal combustion and give one effect.
questions.modelAnswer: It forms during incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited. It is toxic because it reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.
markingPoints: It forms during incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited. It is toxic because it reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

questions.question: State how nitrogen oxides are formed during coal combustion and give one effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Nitrogen and oxygen from air react at high temperatures. Nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and respiratory problems.
markingPoints: Nitrogen and oxygen from air react at high temperatures. Nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and respiratory problems.

questions.question: State how particulates are formed during coal combustion and give one effect.
questions.modelAnswer: They are tiny solid particles produced by incomplete combustion. They can cause respiratory problems and global dimming.
markingPoints: They are tiny solid particles produced by incomplete combustion. They can cause respiratory problems and global dimming.

questions.question: State how sulfur dioxide is formed during coal combustion and give one effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur impurities in coal react with oxygen. Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and can cause respiratory problems.
markingPoints: Sulfur impurities in coal react with oxygen. Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and can cause respiratory problems.

questions.question: Explain how sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides cause environmental harm and how their emissions can be reduced.
questions.modelAnswer:
They form acidic solutions/acid rain, damaging ecosystems/buildings.
NOx also contributes to respiratory problems/smog.
Use low-sulfur fuels/flue-gas desulfurisation, catalytic converters, lower combustion temperatures and reduced fossil-fuel use.
markingPoints: They form acidic solutions/acid rain, damaging ecosystems/buildings.
NOx also contributes to respiratory problems/smog.
Use low-sulfur fuels/flue-gas desulfurisation, catalytic converters, lower combustion temperatures and reduced fossil-fuel use.

questions.question: State one environmental effect of sulfur dioxide and one of nitrogen oxides.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and photochemical smog/respiratory problems.
markingPoints: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and photochemical smog/respiratory problems.

questions.question: Define carbon footprint.
questions.modelAnswer: The total amount of greenhouse gases released over the full life cycle of a product, service or activity.
markingPoints: The total amount of greenhouse gases released over the full life cycle of a product, service or activity.

questions.question: Evaluate three ways a school could reduce its carbon footprint.
questions.modelAnswer: Any three evaluated methods, for example: reduce energy use by switching off equipment; reduce travel emissions by promoting walking/cycling; reduce waste by reusing and recycling. Credit a relevant limitation or practical consideration for each.
markingPoints: Any three evaluated methods, for example: reduce energy use by switching off equipment; reduce travel emissions by promoting walking/cycling; reduce waste by reusing and recycling. Credit a relevant limitation or practical consideration for each.

questions.question: Describe how to compare particulate pollution at two roadside locations using deposited particles.
questions.modelAnswer:
Expose equal-area collection surfaces for the same time and height.
Use several samples at each site.
Keep weather period comparable.
Count particles or measure covered area with a microscope/image analysis.
Calculate means.
Record traffic and weather as possible confounders.
markingPoints: Expose equal-area collection surfaces for the same time and height.
Use several samples at each site.
Keep weather period comparable.
Count particles or measure covered area with a microscope/image analysis.
Calculate means.
Record traffic and weather as possible confounders.

questions.question: A pollution sensor is calibrated incorrectly and reads 5 ppm too high. Explain why taking more readings does not improve accuracy.
questions.modelAnswer:
All readings have the same systematic positive bias.
More readings may improve precision of the mean but it remains about 5 ppm too high.
Recalibration is needed.
markingPoints: All readings have the same systematic positive bias.
More readings may improve precision of the mean but it remains about 5 ppm too high.
Recalibration is needed.
